hypothesis: Agentic AI systems employing multi-agent architectures—where specialized agents collaboratively reason, design experiments, and iteratively refine outputs—can substantially improve clinical trial design by integrating multimodal patient data, predicting trial outcomes, optimizing drug candidates, and simulating preclinical evaluations, thereby reducing the high costs and failure rates associated with traditional trial development. As these systems evolve from automated research assistants toward fully autonomous scientific partners, they are poised to address longstanding inefficiencies in trial design such as poor patient stratification and inadequate endpoint definitions. Realizing this potential will require robust ethical oversight, federated agent protocols, and mechanisms for accountability to ensure trustworthy deployment in high-stakes clinical contexts.
